definition: Uncanny means strange in a way that seems to defy natural explanation, with no ordinary cause that can account for it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word uncanny. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know uncanny should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: There was something uncanny about the antique doll in the shop window; no matter where visitors stood, its painted eyes seemed to follow them across the room.
Something odd is merely a bit strange, while something uncanny is strange in a way that raises the hairs on the back of your neck.
An uncanny event feels almost beyond explanation, but a supernatural one openly breaks the laws of nature.

Eerie describes strangeness felt as fear: a ghostly, frightening atmosphere, whatever its cause. Uncanny adds a stricter test — the strangeness seems to defy natural explanation, the way a guess that proves impossibly exact does. Something eerie scares you; something uncanny also puzzles you.

Unnerving means making someone lose their calm, and anything can do it: a near miss, a long stare, a sudden drop. Uncanny points at one particular source of unease — a strangeness that seems to slip past natural explanation altogether.

Otherworldly describes what seems to belong beyond the natural world entirely, like light or music too perfect for earth. Uncanny stays in this world: an uncanny event happens among ordinary things, yet resists every ordinary explanation you try on it.

Long after the twins had been assigned to cabins on opposite ends of the lake, their camp counselors kept noticing something uncanny: the girls would start humming the same tune at the same moment, as if some invisible signal passed between them across the water.
The twins' perfectly matched behavior feels mysterious and a little unsettling, beyond ordinary coincidence, which is what makes it uncanny.

Uncanny describes strangeness with an unsettling, almost supernatural edge, as in 'an uncanny resemblance' or 'an uncanny ability.' Save it for things that give you a small shiver; something that is merely different or quirky is not uncanny.

Marisol Vega, a records clerk in a small claims office, developed a reputation the statisticians upstairs refused to believe.
Handed any misfiled folder, she could say which of the building's nine hundred cabinets it had strayed from — before opening it, before reading a single label.
An auditor named Pruitt set out to debunk the trick.
He shuffled folders, changed covers, and wore gloves so she could take no cue from him.
Over forty trials she erred twice.
Pruitt checked for marked corners, for smells, for patterns in the paper, and found nothing; her accuracy, he finally wrote, was uncanny.
It happened in an ordinary office, among ordinary cabinets — it simply outran every explanation he tried.
